beats.headline: Is your code just a bag of getters and setters?
beats.subline: Anemic models are the silent killer of enterprise software quality.
beats.narration: If your business rules are scattered across service classes while your entities are just bags of data, you have an anemic domain model. Let's fix that with tactical DDD.

beats.title: Anemic vs. Rich Domain Models
beats.narration: Anemic models let any caller corrupt your state. Rich models encapsulate logic, ensuring that an object is always in a valid state by design.

beats.title: Value Objects with Java Records

steps.explanation: Records are perfect for Value Objects. They are immutable and provide value-based equality automatically.
Validate business invariants at the moment of creation. If it exists, it is valid.

beats.narration: Use Java records for Value Objects. They are immutable, thread-safe, and their compact constructor guarantees that invalid data never enters your system.

beats.title: Tactical DDD Building Blocks
beats.narration: Tactical DDD gives you three tools: Value Objects for attributes, Entities for identity, and Aggregates to enforce consistency across the whole cluster.

beats.title: Part 1 Locked In
takeaways: Records are perfect for Value Objects
beats.nextPartTeaser: Up Next (Part 2): Protecting invariants with Aggregate Roots →
beats.narration: That is the foundation. In Part 2, we build a self-validating Aggregate Root that makes illegal states impossible.

beats.headline: Can your Order exist with zero items?
beats.subline: If it can, your Aggregate Root is leaking business logic.
beats.narration: If your code allows an order to be confirmed while empty, you have failed to protect your invariants. Let's build a proper Aggregate Root.

beats.title: Protecting Aggregate Invariants

steps.explanation: Check status first to prevent illegal state transitions.
Validate business rules before modifying any internal state.

beats.narration: The Aggregate Root is the gatekeeper. Always validate invariants before touching state. If a check fails, the aggregate remains in its previous valid state.

beats.title: Aggregate Design Rules
beats.narration: Follow these four rules: interact only through the root, enforce invariants, reference other aggregates by ID only, and modify one aggregate per transaction.

beats.title: Repository vs. DAO
beats.narration: Repositories are not DAOs. A DAO manages table rows; a Repository manages the lifecycle of an entire Aggregate. Never expose child entities for direct deletion.

beats.title: Part 2 Locked In
beats.nextPartTeaser: Up Next (Part 3): Decoupling with Domain Events →
beats.narration: That is how you maintain consistency. In Part 3, we use Domain Events to decouple your services without losing transactional integrity.

beats.headline: Are your services tangled in a web of dependencies?
beats.subline: Stop calling downstream services directly inside your transactions.
beats.narration: Calling three different services inside one transaction is a recipe for disaster. Use Domain Events to keep your bounded contexts clean and decoupled.

beats.title: Capturing Domain Facts

steps.explanation: Record what happened, not what should happen next.
Collect events inside the aggregate, pull them after saving.

beats.narration: Domain events capture facts that occurred. By buffering them in the aggregate, you can publish them safely after the transaction commits.

beats.title: Safe Event Dispatch
beats.narration: Never publish events before the transaction commits. Use an Outbox table or post-commit listeners to ensure downstream systems don't receive phantom events.

beats.title: Outbox Pattern Logic
beats.caption: Ensuring event delivery

lines.text: 1. Save aggregate + event in one transaction

beats.narration: For mission-critical events, write to an Outbox table in the same transaction as your aggregate. A separate relay process then handles the asynchronous delivery.

beats.title: Part 3 Locked In
beats.narration: You are now decoupling like a pro. In Part 4, we protect your domain from legacy system rot using Anti-Corruption Layers.

beats.headline: Is your domain code full of legacy ERP hacks?
beats.subline: Stop letting messy external APIs pollute your clean domain model.
beats.narration: If your domain logic is littered with legacy ERP codes like STS_01, you need an Anti-Corruption Layer. Let's isolate the mess.

beats.title: Implementing an ACL

steps.explanation: Define what the domain needs, not what the legacy system provides.
Map legacy DTOs to your clean domain types here.

beats.narration: The ACL is a translator. It consumes messy legacy data and maps it to your domain's clean types. Your domain services never see the legacy mess.

beats.title: ACL Isolation Architecture
beats.narration: The ACL acts as a barrier. If the legacy system changes its API, you only update the adapter. Your domain model remains untouched.

beats.title: Direct Integration vs. ACL
beats.narration: Direct integration forces your domain to know about legacy quirks. The ACL pattern keeps your business logic clean and focused on the problem at hand.

beats.title: Chapter Complete!
beats.narration: You have mastered tactical DDD. Checkout the companion branch to run the lab and see these patterns in a real-world project.
